title: Higher Judicial Appointments
lead: ==Arts 124/217==: the President appoints SC/HC judges ==in consultation with the CJI==. The ==Collegium System== is a judicial evolution supplemented by the ==Memorandum of Procedure==; the CJI is chosen ==by seniority, by convention==.

head: Milestone
What it settled
rows: [[UoI v. Sankalchand Sheth (1977)]]
==‘Consultation’ is not concurrence==; limited court review if advice not followed.
[[S.P. Gupta v. President of India (1981)]] — ==1st Judges Case==
Consultation ≠ concurrence; the ==court reduced its own power==; review only on ==mala fide== rejection.
[[SC AoR Assn v. UoI (1993)]] — ==2nd Judges Case==
Introduced the ==Collegium System== with ==primacy to the CJI==; overruled earlier judgments.
[[In Re: Presidential Reference (1999)]] — ==3rd Judges Case==
‘Consultation’ means ==plurality==: ==CJI + 4 senior SC judges== (SC); ==CJI + 2 senior HC judges== (HC).
==99th CA + NJAC==
CJI + 2 senior SC judges + Law Minister + 2 eminent jurists nominated by CJI, PM and LoP (one from SC/ST/OBC, religious minority or woman).
[[SC AoR Assn v. UoI (2015)]] — ==4th Judges Case==
==99th CA and NJAC struck down== — independence of the judiciary is basic structure.

items: ==Lack of transparency== — resolutions unpublished until 2017; even now they convey the decision without the ==comparative assessment== of candidates.
==Executive influence== — the 99th CA route was struck down, leaving the tension unresolved.
==Merit vs representation== — ==no publicly measurable, uniformly applied indicators== of ‘merit’ for elevation from the Bar.
==Accountability== — post-NJAC the SC itself suggested a ==formal complaints mechanism== in the MoP.
==Diversity deficit== — a ==2023 Parliamentary Standing Committee== report found only ~==3% SC and 1.5% ST== among HC judges appointed since 2018.
==Informal lobbying and nepotism== — from May 2025 the SC began publishing whether recommended HC candidates are ==related to serving/retired judges==.
==Delays== — as of 1 July 2026, ==1,122 sanctioned vs 781 working== HC judges: ==341 vacancies, ~30%==.

items.title: Recommendations
bullets: Publish ==fuller collegium details== (SC and now HC)
==At least one woman judge== in the collegium regardless of seniority
==‘Eminent jurists’== to also be appointed to the SC
A dedicated ==Office of Judicial Appointments== within the SC

items.title: Global Best Practices
bullets: ==US==: President appoints with ==Senate consent==; candidates assessed by an ==American Bar Association committee==, reviewed by the Senate Judiciary Committee; ==no retirement age== — office held during good behaviour
==UK==: an independent ==Judicial Appointments Commission== of 15 — three judges, ==12 by open competition==
==South Africa==: a ==23-member Judicial Services Commission== advises the President

blocks.text: In a constitutional democracy, the question is not merely who appoints the judges, but who guards the independence, integrity and legitimacy of those who guard the Constitution.

head: Type
Supreme Court
High Court
rows: ==Ad hoc==

==Art 127== — for shortage/quorum. Eligibility: sitting HC judge qualified for the SC. ==Same status as an SC judge==, temporary. Process: President's consent, consultation with the HC Chief Justice, ==CJI's written request==.

==Art 224A== (added by the ==15th CA, 1963==) — no reason specified in the Constitution. Eligibility: ==ex-HC judge==. Similar benefits, ==not deemed== an HC judge. Process: HC Chief Justice with President's consent.
==Retired==
==Art 128== — no reason specified. Eligibility: ex-SC judge, or ex-HC judge qualified for the SC. Similar benefits, not deemed an SC judge. Process: ==CJI with President's consent==.
==Additional==
==Art 224(1)== — for increase/backlog. Qualified to be an HC judge; ==same status==. Period: ==2 years max or age 62==. Appointed by the President.
==Acting==
==Art 224(2)== — sitting HC judge unavailable. Same status; until the sitting judge returns or age 62. Appointed by the President.

blocks.text: When the process of appointing judges lacks transparency, the credibility of justice itself stands trial. A judiciary meant to be the guardian of the Constitution cannot draw its strength from shadows.
